q-334640.name: Question 1
q-334640.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=2x-3xy \\ {y}^{′}=-5y+4xy\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Find the nonzero equilibrium of the model.

$(${{field-1}}
$,$
{{field-2}}$)$
q-334640.worked_solution:
The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system ${x}^{′}(t)=f(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=0.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2x-3xy=0 \\ -5y+4xy=0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-3xy & =0 \\ x(2-3y) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $x=0$ or $y=\frac{2}{3}.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $x=0,$ substituting it into the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-5y+4(0)y=0\,⇒\,y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, one equilibrium is $(0,0).$

- If $y=\frac{2}{3},$ substituting it into the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-5y+4xy & =0 \\ y(-5+4x) & =0 \\ \frac{2}{3}(-5+4x) & =0 \\ -5+4x & =0 \\ x & =\frac{5}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $(\frac{5}{4},\frac{2}{3}).$

Therefore, the nonzero equilibrium of the model is
$(\frac{5}{4},\frac{2}{3}).$

q-335008.name: Question 3
q-335008.problem:
$$ \{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=4x-2xy \\ {y}^{′}=-3y+5xy\end{aligned} $$ Consider the Lotka-Volterra model above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Select the correct options in the reasoning below.$\,$ Evaluating the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0,\,0]^{T},$ we get
$J({x}^{∗})=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} $\,.$
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
$\,$ The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are {{field-5}}. $\,$ Therefore, the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}$ is {{field-6}}{{field-7}}.
q-335008.worked_solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=4x-2xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=-3y+5xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x-2xy)=4-2y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x-2xy)=-2x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3y+5xy)=5y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3y+5xy)=-3+5x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=[\begin{aligned}4-2y & -2x \\ 5y & -3+5x\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}4-2(0) & -2(0) \\ 5(0) & -3+5(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=4\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ Since eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is $\text{an unstable}$ $\text{saddle}.$

EXPLANATION

Let's denote f1(x,y)=4x−2xy and f2(x,y)=−3y+5xy.

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

∂f1∂x=∂∂x(4x−2xy)=4−2y,∂f1∂y=∂∂y(4x−2xy)=−2x∂f2∂x=∂∂x(−3y+5xy)=5y,∂f2∂y=∂∂y(−3y+5xy)=−3+5x

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is J=[4−2y−2x5y−3+5x].

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium x∗=[00] to get

J(x∗)=[4−2(0)−2(0)5(0)−3+5(0)]=[400−3].

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are λ1=4 and λ2=−3. Since eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is an unstable saddle.
